e.t: Angi, also written Anggi, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs twice within one verse in the Greek LXX, Numbers 26:24. Its precise significance there comes from the surrounding passage, but its ordinary function is simply to identify the named individual.

This word means acting “injuriously; unjustly”—doing harm or treating someone unfairly. It is an adverb, so it describes how an action is carried out rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used across 26 occurrences, including passages from Leviticus, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and Wisdom. Its repeated use points to conduct that violates what is right, whether through harmful treatment, dishonest dealing, or other unjust action. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “eagle,” the large bird known for powerful flight and keen sight. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament to refer to an eagle or eagles, whether in descriptions of birds, comparisons, or symbolic images. The word occurs 27 times across 27 Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX, showing that it is a recurring biblical term rather than a rare expression. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means being “despondent”—deeply discouraged, disheartened, or cast down. As a verb, it describes a person entering or remaining in a state of low courage rather than naming a permanent identity. It occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, chiefly in Old Testament books, with one occurrence in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is loss of heart and discouragement.

This word means “Egyptian,” referring to a person from Egypt or to something associated with Egypt. It can function as a noun when identifying Egyptians and as an adjective when describing an Egyptian people, place, or matter. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 134 times, especially in Exodus, where Egypt and its people appear prominently in Israel’s history. Its basic meaning remains geographical and ethnic: it identifies what belongs to Egypt or someone who comes from there.

This word means “ill-timed” or “unseasonable”. As an adjective, it describes something occurring at an unsuitable or inappropriate time rather than at the proper moment. It can therefore point to speech, action, or circumstances whose timing makes them unwelcome or ineffective. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains timing that does not fit the occasion.

This adjective describes something cut off sharply, made pointed, or abrupt in its shape or edge. It can refer to a physically sharp object or a form that ends suddenly rather than gradually. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books represented here, it occurs 11 times, including descriptions connected with cutting or sharpness. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains a sharply cut or abrupt form.

This noun means an “outpouring”—something poured out or released in abundance. It describes the result or act of flowing forth, rather than a person or object with a specific identity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Habakkuk and once in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but the central idea remains something issued or poured outward. [p03:word:lxx:L701076:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L701076:occurrences]

This adjective describes people, objects, or positions set face to face—that is, directly opposite one another. It expresses a direct arrangement or encounter rather than something distant or merely related. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across six verses, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Samuel, Chronicles, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being positioned or compared, but its central idea remains direct opposition or correspondence: one side stands directly before the other.

This noun means “effluence” or “emanation”: something flowing or proceeding outward from a source. It describes an outflow rather than the source itself, and it can refer to what comes forth from something in a continuous or expressive way. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:25. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This noun means “excellence” or “prowess”—outstanding ability, strength, or achievement. It describes the quality of someone who performs remarkably well or displays notable power. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 12:16, so its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains recognized distinction through exceptional ability or strength.

“Asobaesd; Asovaezth” is a proper name, functioning as a personal designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise identity must be taken from the surrounding genealogical passage, since the name itself does not provide an ordinary descriptive meaning. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 3:20. The two forms are presented as renderings of the same named entity, not as separate meanings.

Achithalam, also rendered Akhithalam, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular named person or place in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 2:46. Because the available wording gives the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its precise identity and significance must be understood from that passage rather than from the name alone.

This is a proper name identifying “Basanitis,” also rendered “Vasanitis,” in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, from Joshua through Zechariah, including eight occurrences in Joshua. The name itself identifies the term, while the precise reference intended in any verse depends on that passage’s setting.

Beelmōn, also rendered Veelmon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX, in Joshua 13:17. Without the verse text, its precise referent cannot be described further here, but the supplied meaning consistently presents it as a name, not a general vocabulary term.

Berzelli is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered “Berzelli,” with “Verzelli” also given as a gloss, so it functions as a personal name rather than a word describing an idea, action, or quality. The name occurs ten times across nine verses, from 2 Samuel through Nehemiah. Its precise reference depends on the passage.

Gaar is a proper name, rendered as “Gaar.” It functions as a name rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Nehemiah 7:49, so there is no wider usage pattern available for comparison. Its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding passage, since the name itself does not provide that context.

This adjective means “carved,” describing something shaped by cutting or engraving. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings for objects or images made by human workmanship, especially when distinguishing them from what is naturally occurring or divinely given. The word appears 52 times in this corpus, from Exodus through 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the noun it describes and the surrounding passage.

Gomer is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies someone named Gomer. The name appears twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Ezekiel 38:6 and once in Hosea 1:3. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself supports identification but does not establish additional meaning or significance.

This noun means “instructor” or “schoolmaster.” It refers to a person who teaches or guides others in learning. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, all in Deuteronomy, so its recorded use is limited to that book’s contexts. The word describes a teaching role rather than an action or quality. Its precise emphasis in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This is a proper name referring to Daniel, also rendered Thanil. It functions as a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 127 times, most often in Daniel and also in Bel and the Dragon, Susanna, 1 Chronicles, Ezekiel, and 4 Maccabees. The name appears across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books in this LXX corpus.

This adjective describes someone who is timid or intimidated—held back by fear, lack of confidence, or a sense of being overawed. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it is used 23 times, so its basic idea recurs across different situations rather than naming one particular emotion or event. The surrounding verse determines whether the person is fearful, lacking courage, or made afraid by another person or circumstance. It describes a condition or attitude, not an action.

Delanath is a proper name, rendered “Dēlanath” or “Thilanath.” It identifies a named place or location rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Joshua 17:7. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional meaning or explanation of its name. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its geographical context.

e.h: A Word for Steal At Different Times
e.t: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “steal at different times”. It describes stealing that happens on separate occasions, rather than referring only to one isolated act. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, with both occurrences in 2 Samuel 19:4. The surrounding verse determines how this action is expressed there. Its meaning remains focused on repeated or distinct acts of stealing, not on a broader idea.

This verb means to “attempt” or “test”—to try something or put it to the test. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:40. The surrounding verse is needed to determine whether the action emphasizes making an attempt, examining something, or testing someone in that particular setting.

This adjective means “bipartite” or “in two parts.” It describes something divided into, or consisting of, two distinct sections. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Daniel 2:41. The word itself identifies a two-part structure, while the surrounding verse determines what divided or combined thing is being described. It is a descriptive term rather than a name for a person, place, or action.

This noun refers to a kind of deer. In the Greek Old Testament, it names an animal rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs 14 times across the LXX corpus, including passages in Deuteronomy, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, and Song of Songs. Its basic meaning remains zoological: a particular type of deer mentioned in biblical descriptions and comparisons. The surrounding verse determines why the animal is being mentioned, but the word itself identifies the creature.

Ezekias is a proper name—the Greek Old Testament form of a person’s name, not a word describing an action or quality. It identifies King Ezekias, who appears repeatedly in the historical books and in Isaiah, with two further occurrences in Sirach. The name occurs 97 times in the Greek LXX corpus, so its function remains consistent: it points to this individual whenever it appears. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the name itself functions as a personal designation.

This Greek LXX verb means “sail into” or “enter.” It describes movement into a place, with the wording especially suited to arriving by ship or boat. In this corpus it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding verse text would determine whether the emphasis falls on the voyage itself or simply on entering. It is a practical action word describing arrival or passage into a destination.

This noun means a “figure in relief”—a raised or molded representation that stands out from a surface. It refers to a visible form shaped so that its image has depth rather than remaining flat. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Exodus and once in Sirach. Its basic sense is the physical figure itself, while the surrounding passage determines what object or design the figure represents.

This word expresses the necessity of coming: “one must come.” It functions as an adjective describing something required or destined to happen, rather than simply reporting that someone comes. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 6:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning is the requirement that someone come.

This Greek LXX verb means “make apparent/visible; represent.” It describes bringing something into view, making it recognizable, or presenting it so that others can perceive what it is. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including Exodus, Esther, Isaiah, Wisdom, and Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being made visible or represented in the surrounding passage.

This noun means “blotting out” or “destruction”—the removal or wiping away of something until it is gone. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in Ezekiel and Micah, and describes a decisive end rather than a temporary difficulty. As a noun, it names the act or result of being erased, removed, or destroyed. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the act of wiping out or on the destruction that follows.

This verb means to “interrogate; inquire of”—to ask someone for information or seek an answer. It can describe ordinary questioning as well as a serious request for guidance, depending on the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 61 times, showing a repeated action of asking, questioning, or seeking an answer rather than a single specialized act. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on who is asking, whom they address, and what information or guidance they seek.

This adjective describes someone or something as “skillful” or “clever.” It points to ability, competence, or practical intelligence rather than merely identifying a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezra 5:8. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be stated beyond this central meaning. Its basic sense remains a positive description of capable, intelligent action or character.

This verb means to impose something on someone or to inflict something upon them. It describes an action brought forcefully or deliberately against a person or situation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 16 times, including passages from Genesis, 1 Samuel, and other books. The surrounding context determines whether the imposed or inflicted thing is a burden, harm, judgment, or another action; the core idea remains placing something upon someone or causing it to be experienced.

This word means “seven,” the number that comes after six and before eight. It functions as a number used to count people, objects, periods, or repeated occurrences. In the Greek LXX, it appears 329 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it occurs. The surrounding passage determines what is being counted and how the number functions in that sentence.

This adjective describes someone or something marked by wanton behavior or insolence—boldly disrespectful, offensive, or lacking proper restraint. It presents a quality rather than an action, so the surrounding sentence determines exactly whom or what it describes. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:7. Its stated meaning is “wanton; insolent,” and no broader sense is established here.

This Greek LXX noun means “jealousy” or “rivalry”—the troubled concern that another person may possess, receive, or claim what one regards as belonging to oneself. It names an attitude or condition rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Numbers 5, where the term belongs to the law concerning a husband’s jealousy. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is jealousy expressed as suspicion or rivalry.

This word means “leavened,” describing something prepared with leaven rather than left unleavened. It refers to a food made to rise or become fermented through the presence of leaven. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Leviticus 7:13, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though its precise role in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and offering instructions.

This Greek LXX noun means “watercourse,” referring to a channel or stream through which water flows. It appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, all in 1 Kings 18, where the word identifies a physical feature associated with the altar and its surrounding trench. Its basic sense is therefore geographical and concrete: a place or passage carrying water, rather than water considered simply as a substance. The precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “oppression” or “affliction”: suffering imposed on people or endured as a heavy burden. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes distress serious enough to be recognized and brought before God, but its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Exodus 3:9 and once in Deuteronomy 26:7. In both recorded renderings, it is translated “affliction,” reinforcing the sense of painful hardship rather than a minor inconvenience.

This Greek verb means “immolate” or “sacrifice”: to offer something in a sacrificial act. It describes the action of making a sacrifice rather than the offering itself, and it commonly concerns worship offered to God or a deity. The word appears 127 times in the LXX corpus, showing that sacrificial action is a recurring scriptural subject. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context.

This word is a proper name: “Ianoue” or “Ianue.” It identifies a person by name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 3:7. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the name itself does not establish the person’s role, family connection, or significance in that passage.

This proper name refers to Idoumaia, also identified as Ithumea. It functions as a name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it appears 54 times, beginning in Genesis and continuing through 2 Maccabees. Because the supplied material gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its specific role in any particular passage must be understood from that passage’s context.

e.h: Priestly or For the Priest’s Office
e.t: This adjective means “priestly” or “for the priest's office.” It describes something connected with the role or service of a priest, marking it as belonging to priestly use or responsibility rather than describing an ordinary object or activity. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 3:15. The word's precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

This word is a proper name identifying a person, rather than a term describing an action, quality, or object. Its recorded name glosses are “Iēou” and “Iiu.” In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice in 1 Chronicles 2:38, both occurrences appearing in the same verse. The name’s precise role in that genealogy depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here; its basic meaning is simply a personal designation.

This LXX Greek verb means “enjoy the fruits of”: it describes receiving or benefiting from the results or produce connected with something. It is an action word, so it focuses on what someone does with an outcome rather than merely naming the fruit itself. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, in Joshua 5:12 and Proverbs 8:19. The surrounding verse determines whether the phrase points to literal produce or a broader result.

Katanath is a proper name that identifies a named person, place, or other entity rather than describing an action or quality. Its meaning is preserved as the name “Katanath,” so no broader definition is supplied. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 19:15. The surrounding verse would be needed to identify exactly what Katanath names there; the word itself functions as a designation, not as a descriptive term.

This noun means “observation” or a “means of observing”—the act or method of paying attention in order to notice or understand something. It describes observation itself rather than a person who observes or the thing being observed. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 41:23. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains careful attention or the process by which something is examined and understood.

This Greek LXX noun means “settlement” or “settling.” It refers to establishing residence in a place or to the settled condition that results. The word is used 25 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so it can describe places where people live as well as the act of making a home or dwelling. Its exact emphasis—whether the process of settling or the resulting settlement—depends on the sentence in which it appears.

Keblaam, also rendered Kevlaam, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal or place name rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 2 Kings 15:10. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not explain its etymology or identify more specifically what or whom it names. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “cling” or “join”: it describes attaching oneself to someone or something and remaining closely connected. It can express physical attachment, close association, or the act of joining together, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 34 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its central idea is a close bond rather than a brief meeting. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “well” or “spring,” referring to a place or source where water is found. It is a concrete word for a water source, whether described as a constructed well or a natural spring. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and Sirach corpus, appearing across historical accounts and wisdom literature. Its exact sense in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains a well or spring.

Labōemath, also rendered Lavoemath, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. As a proper name, it identifies a particular person, place, or other named entity rather than expressing a general quality or action. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Judges 3:3. The available information establishes its name-function and rendering, but does not identify the named referent beyond that occurrence.

Lydia; Lithia is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name. The gloss gives both “Lydia” and “Lithia” as approved renderings, so the exact English spelling may vary. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 8:8. Without the verse text and surrounding context, its specific reference cannot be identified further, but its basic function is as a name rather than a description or action.

Maspha, also written Masfa, is a proper name used for a place in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies that named location rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. The name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Joshua and once in 2 Chronicles. Because the word is a place-name, its precise significance in either passage comes from the surrounding verse and geographic context, not from a general abstract meaning.

This Greek LXX verb means “fill” or “full of,” describing something becoming filled or being full. It presents fullness as a condition or developing state rather than naming a specific object by itself. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on what is said to be filled and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains fullness or being filled.

This Greek LXX adverb expresses doubt or rejection, meaning “not perhaps; much less.” It can qualify a thought by questioning whether something is possible and then strengthening the denial by saying that an even greater possibility is out of the question. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Daniel 2:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and question.

Misa is a proper name—the personal name of an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the LXX, at 1 Chronicles 8:9. Since the name itself identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object, its basic meaning is simply the person’s name, Misa. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that individual’s place in the genealogy, but the lexical sense remains a personal name.

Micha, also rendered Mikha, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies individuals in genealogical and historical records. This name occurs 11 times across 10 verses, appearing in 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. Its precise reference changes with each passage, but its ordinary function remains that of a person’s name.

Mosolamoth is a proper name preserved as “Mosolamōth” or “Mosolamoth” in the Greek Septuagint. It identifies a person rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. The name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 2 Chronicles 28:12. The available lexical information gives the name’s form but does not provide a further meaning or etymological explanation, so it is best understood simply as the individual’s name in that passage.

This noun means a “diadem” or a “sign of consecration”—a visible headpiece or mark associated with being set apart. It refers to an outward sign of sacred appointment or dedication, rather than describing an ordinary ornament alone. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs once, at 2 Kings 11:12. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene.

This adjective means “eightieth,” describing something that holds the position of number eighty in an ordered sequence. It is an ordinal term, so it identifies rank or place rather than simply expressing the number eighty by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 1:9. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what the adjective describes there.

Oldan, also rendered Olthan, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It appears twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus, once in 2 Kings 22:14 and once in 2 Chronicles 34:22. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its basic meaning is the person’s name itself; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s specific role or actions.

This adverb means “backwards,” describing movement or direction toward the rear rather than forward. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis 9:23. As an adverb, it modifies an action by indicating how or in what direction something is done. Its basic sense is straightforward, while the exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. The word itself focuses on backward direction, not on a separate moral or spiritual idea.

This word means “altogether” or “entirely.” As an adverb, it strengthens a statement by expressing completeness or an unrestricted extent. It can describe something as wholly so, rather than partly or only to a limited degree. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea is totality or complete extent.

This Greek LXX verb means to “fence all round”: to surround something completely with a boundary or enclosure. It describes an action that places something within a guarded or enclosed area, rather than merely touching or approaching it. The word occurs six times in the Greek LXX corpus, across passages from Kings, Job, Sirach, 2 Maccabees, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being enclosed.

This word means a “wine-jar,” a container used for holding wine. It is a noun referring to the vessel itself, not to the wine inside it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 23:27. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a physical jar or container associated with wine.

This adjective describes a person or thing as “longed for” or “desired.” It identifies what is wanted or regarded with longing. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times: once in Proverbs and twice in 4 Maccabees. Its central meaning remains consistent wherever it appears: the person or thing described is wanted. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

πορεία means “travel” or “journey”—the act or course of going from one place to another. It is a noun, so it names the journey itself rather than describing someone’s action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented here, it occurs 28 times. Its range covers ordinary movement from place to place, while the surrounding passage determines the particular journey in view. The word appears across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books in this corpus.

This Greek LXX verb means “spit forth,” describing the act of forcefully ejecting something from the mouth. It presents an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 6:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the outward expulsion expressed by “spit forth.”

This verb means “light up” or “kindle,” describing the act of causing something to burn or give light. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in Proverbs. Its wording points to an active process: something is ignited, stirred into flame, or made brighter. The surrounding verse determines whether the immediate subject is a literal fire or a figurative kindling, but the central idea remains setting something alight or causing it to glow.

Respha, also rendered Rhesfa, is a proper name referring to a woman named in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but a personal designation. This name occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, all in 2 Samuel: 2 Samuel 3:7; 21:8, 10, and 11. The name’s precise significance in any one passage comes from the surrounding account, but its basic meaning here is the personal name Respha.

This noun means “pack” or “baggage,” referring to the belongings or load that someone carries. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 2 Maccabees 3:25. Its basic sense is practical and concrete: a bundle of possessions or equipment transported from one place to another. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how the word functions there, but the word itself points to carried belongings rather than an action or personal quality.

Sama is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, each time in a different verse. The name is found once in 1 Samuel and three times in 1 Chronicles, including references to people listed in Israel’s history and family records. Since no fuller definition is given for the name itself, its precise identity in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Sava is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both in Genesis 38, and is rendered “Sava.” The name appears in Genesis 38:2 and Genesis 38:12. Its lexical meaning is therefore the personal designation “Sava”; any further significance depends on the surrounding passage, not on the name itself.

This verb means “take food; eat.” It describes the ordinary act of consuming food, rather than naming a meal or a person who eats. In the LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the action of eating or taking nourishment. It is a straightforward action word with a practical, bodily sense.

This word means “myrrh oil,” a fragrant oil or substance known in the Old Testament Greek Scriptures. It is a noun naming this valuable aromatic material. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Kings, Psalms, and Song of Songs. Its uses range across ordinary valuable goods, offerings, and pleasant fragrance, while the surrounding verse determines its precise role. It is distinct from the Greek New Testament vocabulary and belongs specifically to the Greek translation of the Old Testament.

This Greek LXX noun means “convergence,” referring to people, things, or movements coming together at one point. It describes a gathering or meeting rather than an individual object or action. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 3:8. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains the joining or assembling of separate things into one place or meeting.

This LXX adjective means “thirtieth,” describing something that holds the ordinal position of number thirty. It identifies a place in a sequence, such as the thirtieth year, day, person, or item, depending on the noun it describes. The word appears 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including historical books and 1 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains a straightforward numerical designation rather than a description of quality, action, or character.

gl: of three years; three years old
d: of three years; three years old

e.t: This word means “of three years” or “three years old.” It describes a person, animal, or thing in relation to an age of three years, and it can function as either a noun or an adjective. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: twice in the Old Testament and twice in 2 Maccabees. Its basic meaning is straightforward; the surrounding verse determines what is three years old or what three-year period is being described.

This word means “officiate; serve.” It is a verb describing the act of carrying out service or performing a duty. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs five times, all in the deuterocanonical books represented here: four times in Wisdom and once in Sirach. Its central idea is active service—someone functioning in a serving role rather than merely being identified as a servant. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “give an example” or “indicate”—to make something clear by pointing it out or showing it as a model. It can describe directing someone’s attention to a matter or presenting an example that helps explain what is intended. The word occurs 37 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its central idea is an action of showing, identifying, or demonstrating rather than merely mentioning something.

This adjective describes someone who owes a debt or is under an obligation to repay what is owed. It means “indebted” or “in debt,” pointing to a person’s financial or duty-bound obligation rather than simply describing poverty. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 1 Samuel 22:2 and once in Isaiah 50:1. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This adjective describes something as “fearful” or “fearsome”—something that inspires fear or has a terrifying character. It functions as a describing word, rather than naming a person, place, or action by itself. The term occurs 36 times in the Greek LXX corpus, showing repeated use for things regarded as deeply alarming or awe-inspiring. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “rough; shudder.” It describes a trembling or shuddering response, while “rough” is also part of its recorded lexical sense. In the LXX corpus, it occurs only twice, both in 4 Maccabees, and both occurrences are rendered “shudder.” Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is a physical reaction of shuddering or becoming rough.

“For thanksgiving” describes something intended for giving thanks. As an adjective, the word identifies an object or action connected with thanksgiving rather than naming thanksgiving itself. Its meaning is functional: it points to something used or designated in relation to thankful praise. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:45. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what it modifies there.

Chelia, also rendered Khelia, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:35. The available lexical meaning identifies it as the name itself; the supplied information does not provide additional details about the person who bore it or the significance of the name. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

Cholaseōla, also rendered Cholaseola, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or locality in the Greek Old Testament wording of Joshua. The name occurs once in this corpus, at Joshua 15:28. Without the verse’s surrounding text, its precise location or significance cannot be explained further, but its basic function is to designate that particular named place.

This word means “bare,” describing something exposed or without a covering. It is an adjective, so it describes a person or thing rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 7:21. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic idea remains clear: something is presented without the covering or addition that might otherwise be expected. The word itself does not explain why it is bare.
